p: Which statement about OpenConfig models on IOS XE is accurate?
o: They're vendor-neutral, and IOS XE publishes deviation modules for the nodes it doesn't implement
They're vendor-neutral, but IOS XE can only advertise them if it implements every node in each model
They're published by the IETF, and IOS XE publishes deviation modules for the nodes it doesn't implement
They're vendor-neutral, but configuration applied through them can't be read back through the native model
e: OpenConfig is written by an operator group, not the IETF. IOS XE translates OpenConfig configuration into its own running configuration, so the native model can read it, and deviation modules mark the unsupported nodes.

p: Which body for POST /restconf/data/example-qos:policies creates policy EDGE with class 10 set to drop, applied to Gi1 and Gi2?
o: `{"example-qos:policy": [{"name": "EDGE", "class": [{"id": 10, "drop": true}], "applies-to": ["Gi1", "Gi2"]}]}`
`{"example-qos:policy": [{"name": "EDGE", "class": [{"id": 10, "drop": null}], "applies-to": ["Gi1", "Gi2"]}]}`
`{"example-qos:policy": [{"name": "EDGE", "class": [{"id": 10, "drop": [null]}], "applies-to": ["Gi1", "Gi2"]}]}`
`{"example-qos:policy": [{"name": "EDGE", "class": [{"id": 10, "action": {"drop": [null]}}], "applies-to": ["Gi1", "Gi2"]}]}`
e: RFC 7951 encodes a leaf of type empty as [null]. Choice and case names never appear in data, so drop sits directly in the class entry. uint8 values are JSON numbers.
c:
module: example-qos
  +--rw policies
     +--rw policy* [name]
        +--rw name          string
        +--rw class* [id]
        |  +--rw id         uint8
        |  +--rw (action)?
        |     +--:(drop)
        |     |  +--rw drop?   empty
        |     +--:(mark)
        |        +--rw dscp?   uint8
        +--rw applies-to*   string

p: The module's namespace is urn:example:sys. The edit must clear location whether or not it's currently set, without returning an error. Which `<config>` content does that?
o: `<system xmlns="urn:example:sys" xmlns:nc="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:netconf:base:1.0"><location nc:operation="delete"/></system>`
`<system xmlns="urn:example:sys" xmlns:nc="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:netconf:base:1.0"><location nc:operation="none"/></system>`
`<system xmlns="urn:example:sys"><location operation="remove"/></system>`
`<system xmlns="urn:example:sys" xmlns:nc="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:netconf:base:1.0"><location nc:operation="remove"/></system>`
e: remove deletes the node if it exists and does nothing if it doesn't. delete returns data-missing when the node is absent. The attribute must be in the NETCONF base namespace, and none makes no change.
c:
module: example-sys
  +--rw system
     +--rw contact?    string
     +--rw location?   string

p: Which RESTCONF request runs reset on Gi1 with counters-only set?
o: `PUT /restconf/data/example-if:interfaces/interface=Gi1/reset` with {"example-if:input": {"counters-only": true}}
`POST /restconf/operations/example-if:reset` with {"example-if:input": {"name": "Gi1", "counters-only": true}}
`POST /restconf/data/example-if:interfaces/interface=Gi1/reset` with {"example-if:input": {"counters-only": true}}
`POST /restconf/data/example-if:interfaces/interface=Gi1/reset` with {"example-if:reset": {"counters-only": true}}
e: reset sits inside a list entry, so it's a YANG 1.1 action. Actions are invoked with POST on the data resource path, while top-level RPCs use /restconf/operations. The body wraps the parameters in module:input.
c:
module: example-if
  +--rw interfaces
     +--rw interface* [name]
        +--rw name      string
        +--ro errors?   uint32
        +---x reset
           +---w input
           |  +---w counters-only?   boolean
           +--ro output
              +--ro cleared?   uint32

p: Which two statements about this tree are true? (Choose two.)
o: A client can set state to idle to reset a neighbor's session
shutdown takes the value true or false, and defaults to false
router-id must be set before any neighbor can be created
Creating a neighbor requires both address and remote-as
bfd means something when it exists, even with no children
e: remote-as has no ? marker, so it's mandatory, and ! marks a presence container. router-id is optional and independent, state is ro (read-only), and an empty leaf is either present or absent; it has no value.
c:
module: example-bgp
  +--rw bgp
     +--rw asn          inet:as-number
     +--rw router-id?   inet:ipv4-address
     +--rw neighbor* [address]
     |  +--rw address     inet:ip-address
     |  +--rw remote-as   inet:as-number
     |  +--rw shutdown?   empty
     |  +--ro state?      enumeration
     +--rw bfd!

p: Which except clause catches a wrong password for one device, but still lets an unreachable device fall through to the next handler?
o: except NetmikoAuthenticationException
except (NetmikoAuthenticationException, NetmikoTimeoutException)
except ConnectionRefusedError
except NetmikoTimeoutException
e: Netmiko raises NetmikoAuthenticationException for rejected credentials and NetmikoTimeoutException when the host can't be reached. Catching both in the first clause would put unreachable devices on the auth list.

p: The command prompts with Destination filename [startup-config]?. Which code saves the configuration without hanging?
o: out = conn.send_command("copy running-config startup-config", read_timeout=60)

```
out = conn.send_command("copy running-config startup-config", expect_string=r"#")
out += conn.send_command("\n", expect_string=r"Destination filename")
```
out = conn.send_config_set(["copy running-config startup-config", "\n"])

```

out += conn.send_command("\n", expect_string=r"#")
```
e: send_command waits for the normal prompt, which never appears while the device is asking a question. expect_string tells it what to wait for, and the second call answers with Enter. send_config_set would run the command in configuration mode.

p: Why does findall return an empty list here, although the reply contains interfaces?
o: The elements are namespace-qualified, so the search needs the namespace URI or a prefix map
get only returns configuration, so the reply holds no oper-status values to find
The subtree filter must also select interface in a `<filter>` element, or nothing is returned
data_ele is a string, so findall searches its characters rather than any of its elements
e: lxml matches qualified names. Use root.findall(".//if:interface", {"if": "http://cisco.com/ns/yang/Cisco-IOS-XE-interfaces-oper"}) or the {uri}interface form. get returns state data, and data_ele is an element.
c:
FLT = """
<interfaces xmlns="http://cisco.com/ns/yang/Cisco-IOS-XE-interfaces-oper">
  <interface><name/><oper-status/></interface>
</interfaces>"""

reply = m.get(filter=("subtree", FLT))
root = reply.data_ele
for intf in root.findall(".//interface"):
    print(intf.findtext("name"), intf.findtext("oper-status"))

p: What does error_option="rollback-on-error" do in this call?
o: If any part fails, the device skips it and still applies the rest of the edit
If any part fails, processing stops at that point, and changes made before the error stay in place
If any part fails, the device rolls back to the configuration of its last commit
If any part of the edit fails, the whole edit is undone, so the datastore doesn't change
e: rollback-on-error makes the edit atomic and needs the :rollback-on-error capability. stop-on-error keeps earlier changes, continue-on-error skips failures, and neither touches earlier commits.
c:
m.edit_config(target="candidate", config=CFG,
              error_option="rollback-on-error")

p: A GET on /restconf/data/ietf-interfaces:interfaces-state must return only each interface's name and oper-status. Which query does that?
o: ?fields=interface[name;oper-status]
?depth=2&fields=name;oper-status
?fields=interface/name;oper-status
?fields=interface(name;oper-status)
e: In fields, ; separates siblings, / walks down a path, and parentheses apply a selection under one node. interface/name;oper-status would ask for oper-status at the top level, beside interface.

p: A RESTCONF POST creates a new list entry and returns 201 Created. Where does the response give the URL of the new resource?
o: Nowhere, so the client must build the URL from the key
In the Location header
In the body, under ietf-restconf:location
In the ETag header
e: RFC 8040 returns 201 with a Location header pointing at the new resource. ETag identifies a version of a resource, and the body of a successful POST is empty.

p: The device's MGMT ACL differs from these lines by one entry. What does the task send?
o: Nothing, because match: exact only reports differences without changing them
no ip access-list extended MGMT, then only the entry that differs
no ip access-list extended MGMT, then the parent and both lines
The parent and only the entry that differs, without the before line
e: With match: exact, any difference means the whole block is pushed, and before runs first whenever a change is needed. That rebuilds the ACL cleanly.
c:
- name: Enforce the MGMT ACL
  cisco.ios.ios_config:
    parents: ip access-list extended MGMT
    lines:
      - 10 permit tcp 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.255 any eq 22
      - 20 deny ip any any log
    before: no ip access-list extended MGMT
    match: exact

p: This ZTP script runs on a switch whose serial number isn't in CONFIGS. What happens?
o: The lookup raises KeyError, so configurep never runs
configurep applies an empty list and saves the configuration
re.search returns None, so .group(1) raises AttributeError before the lookup
CONFIGS[serial] returns None, so configurep runs with nothing to apply and returns
e: Indexing a dict with a missing key raises KeyError. The serial line is found, so the regex succeeds. Use CONFIGS.get(serial) with a fallback to handle unknown switches.
c:
import cli, re

CONFIGS = {"FOC2233X0AB": ["hostname BR21-SW1", "ip domain name corp.example"]}

def main():
    # Purpose: apply the configuration that matches this switch's serial number
    ver = cli.cli("show version")
    serial = re.search(r"System Serial Number\s+:\s+(\S+)", ver).group(1)
    cli.configurep(CONFIGS[serial])

main()

p: A NETCONF session to IOS XE opens, and get-config works, but every edit-config returns access-denied. What's the most likely cause?
o: The candidate datastore isn't enabled, so writes to running are refused
The user doesn't have privilege 15, so NACM denies write access
The script set hostkey_verify=False, which limits the session to reads
netconf-yang is listening on a port other than 830
e: IOS XE applies NACM rules. Privilege 15 users get full access, and others are denied by default. A missing candidate gives a different error, and port and host key settings affect connecting, not authorization.

p: What does this applet do?
o: Every 5 minutes, it logs Gi1/0/1's CRC counter, whatever its value
Once, 300 seconds after the applet is registered, it logs Gi1/0/1's CRC counter
Every 5 minutes, it logs a warning if Gi1/0/1's CRC counter is above 100
Every 5 minutes, it logs a warning if Gi1/0/1's CRC counter rose by more than 100 since its last run
e: watchdog repeats every 300 seconds (countdown would run once). The regexp stores the number in crc, and the nested if only logs when it exceeds 100. Nothing tracks the previous value, so it compares the total, not the increase.
c:
event manager applet CHECK-CRC
 event timer watchdog time 300
 action 1.0 cli command "enable"
 action 2.0 cli command "show interfaces GigabitEthernet1/0/1 | include CRC"
 action 3.0 regexp "([0-9]+) CRC" "$_cli_result" match crc
 action 4.0 if $_regexp_result eq "1"
 action 5.0  if $crc gt "100"
 action 6.0   syslog priority warnings msg "Gi1/0/1 CRC errors: $crc"
 action 7.0  end
 action 8.0 end

p: Which two statements about Guest Shell on a Catalyst 9000 switch are true? (Choose two.)
o: The switch's bootflash is available inside it under /flash
It has root access to the IOS XE kernel and can change IOSd's memory
Its Python can only call the cli module, not general libraries
It's a Linux container with Python 3, and pip can install packages when it has network access
It runs inside IOSd, so a script crash reloads the switch
e: Guest Shell is an isolated IOx container, so a script crash doesn't affect IOSd. It mounts bootflash at /flash, and it runs ordinary Python with pip.

p: A playbook calls the Meraki API with uri for 200 networks, run as inventory hosts, and many tasks fail with 429. Which two changes help? (Choose two.)
o: Raise timeout to 120 seconds on the task
Limit concurrency with throttle on the task, or use fewer forks
Add validate_certs: false to speed up each call
Retry on 429 with until, retries and a delay
Switch the calls from GET to POST
e: Meraki limits each organization to a few requests per second. Fewer parallel calls and retries after a pause address that. TLS settings and timeouts don't affect the rate limit.

p: Which two statements about VPNs in Catalyst SD-WAN are true? (Choose two.)
o: VPN 0 is reserved for out-of-band management
VPN 512 carries user traffic between sites
Service VPNs such as VPN 10 keep a segment's routes separate across the fabric
All service VPNs share one routing table on each edge
VPN 0 is the transport VPN that faces the WAN
e: VPN 0 connects to the WAN transports, and VPN 512 is for out-of-band management. Each service VPN has its own routing table, end to end.

p: A script logs in to Catalyst Center with an Observer account. GET requests work, but POST /dna/intent/api/v1/network-device returns 403. What's the cause?
o: The token has expired and must be refreshed
The account's role doesn't allow write operations
The script exceeded the API rate limit
The body was sent without Content-Type: application/json
e: 403 means the caller is authenticated but not authorized. Observer is read-only. An expired token gives 401, rate limiting gives 429, and a media type problem gives 415 or 400.

p: A PUT to a REST API succeeds, but r.json() then raises JSONDecodeError. What's the most likely reason?
o: The response is 204 No Content, so there's no body to parse
requests can't parse JSON from a PUT response
The response is 201 Created, and its body is XML by default
The PUT failed silently, and the body holds an HTML error page
e: Many APIs, including RESTCONF, answer a successful PUT with 204 and an empty body. Check r.status_code, or r.content, before calling r.json().

p: After a reboot test, genie diff shows hundreds of changes in counters and uptime, which hide the real differences. What's the best fix?

Run genie learn twice and diff only the second pair of snapshots
Exclude those keys from the comparison, for example Diff(before, after, exclude=["counters", "uptime"])
Clear the counters before the second learn, so they match
e: Diff takes an exclude list of keys that change on their own. Running config ignores the operational state the test is meant to check, and clearing counters still leaves uptime and timers.

o: upgradeWindow.version, which applies to every product in the network
products.switch.currentVersion.id, set to the version wanted next
products.switch.nextUpgrade.toVersion.id, taken from the network's availableVersions
products.switch.nextUpgrade.toVersion.firmware, set to the image file name
e: Each product has a nextUpgrade with a time and a toVersion ID chosen from availableVersions. The upgrade window sets when upgrades happen, not which version.

p: A report needs loss, latency and jitter per tunnel over the last hour, aggregated, from SD-WAN Manager. Which approach fits?
o: `GET /dataservice/device/bfd/sessions` on each edge every few seconds for an hour, then average the samples
POST a query with a time range and grouping to /dataservice/statistics/approute/aggregation
`GET /dataservice/device/control/connections` for each edge
`GET /dataservice/alarms` filtered on the last hour
e: Statistics endpoints take a query in the body and return stored data, with aggregation done by the Manager. BFD sessions are real-time status, control connections cover the control plane, and alarms are events.

p: Which header authenticates a request to the ThousandEyes API v7?
o: `Authorization: Bearer <OAuth bearer token>`
`Authorization: Basic <email:API token>`
`X-Auth-Token: <OAuth bearer token>`
`X-TE-Key: <API token>`
e: API v7 uses a bearer token created in the ThousandEyes account settings. Basic authentication with email and token belongs to the older v6 API.

p: Which value fills the blank so this configured subscription sends data every 30 seconds?
e: The period is in centiseconds, so 30 seconds is 3000. The same units apply in the CLI's update-policy periodic and in NETCONF.

p: show telemetry ietf subscription 301 reports the subscription as Valid, but its receiver as Disconnected, and the collector gets nothing. Which two could cause this? (Choose two.)
o: The XPath filter selects a path that this stream doesn't support for periodic updates
An ACL, route or the source VRF stops the switch reaching the collector
The period is too short for kvgpb encoding
The collector isn't listening on the configured address and port
The subscription needs a NETCONF session to stay open
e: A Valid subscription with a Disconnected receiver means the dial-out connection fails. A bad XPath would make the subscription Invalid, and configured subscriptions don't depend on a NETCONF session.

p: A Meraki network must send alerts to a receiver that expects a different JSON layout from Meraki's default. What fits best?
o: Use the syslog server setting instead, which lets you define the JSON fields
Ask Meraki support to change the payload layout for the organization
Have the receiver call the Dashboard API for each alert, then rebuild the payload in the layout it expects
Create a webhook payload template that formats the alert, and assign it to the webhook server
e: Payload templates, written in Liquid and managed through the Dashboard or the API, reshape the webhook body for each receiver. Syslog sends text messages, not custom JSON.

p: Where are ThousandEyes alerts set up to POST to a custom HTTPS receiver?
o: As a webhook integration, selected in the notifications of an alert rule
In the test's agent settings, as a second target
Through a Catalyst Center event subscription
As a dashboard widget that streams to a URL
e: Webhook integrations define the receiver, and alert rules choose which integrations get notified when they trigger.

p: An admin with read-only Meraki access asks the AI Assistant to change an SSID's password. What should happen?
o: The assistant makes the change and notifies the organization's full admins
The assistant can't take actions of any kind, for any admin
The assistant makes the change, because it runs with its own full-admin rights
The assistant can't make changes beyond the admin's own permissions
e: AI assistants act within the user's role. An assistant with rights the user lacks would be a privilege escalation path.

p: Which Catalyst Center capability runs automated troubleshooting workflows, such as checking devices against security advisories, using a knowledge base of expert reasoning?
o: AI Endpoint Analytics
Software Image Management
The Machine Reasoning Engine
Path Trace
e: The Machine Reasoning Engine powers the Network Reasoner workflows. Endpoint Analytics classifies devices, SWIM manages images, and Path Trace maps a flow's route.

p: An AI-generated function passes a review test with Loopback1 but fails in production. Which test case would have caught the bug, and what's the fix?
o: A name with slashes, such as GigabitEthernet1/0/1; build the URL with quote(name)
A name with slashes, such as GigabitEthernet1/0/1; pass it with params={"name": name}
A longer name, such as TenGigabitEthernet1/1/1; raise the request timeout so long names don't time out
A name with slashes, such as GigabitEthernet1/0/1; build the URL with quote(name, safe="")
e: urllib.parse.quote leaves / unencoded by default (safe="/"), so only safe="" produces %2F. RESTCONF keys belong in the path, not the query string.
c:
def get_intf(base, auth, name):
    # Purpose: read one interface over RESTCONF
    url = f"{base}/data/ietf-interfaces:interfaces/interface={name}"
    r = requests.get(url, auth=auth, verify="corp-ca.pem",
                     headers={"Accept": "application/yang-data+json"})
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()

p: Which two are effective ways to check an API call that an AI assistant suggested? (Choose two.)
o: Ask the assistant whether it's sure about the call
Check that the code passes a formatter without changes
Compare it with the platform's API reference for your release
Run it against a sandbox or lab instance and inspect the response
Accept it if several AI answers, from different assistants, suggest the same call
e: Documentation and real responses are independent evidence. Self-checks and agreement between AI answers can repeat the same mistake, and formatting says nothing about correctness.

p: An LLM summarizes syslog for the NOC and can also open change tickets and run show commands through tools. Which two controls limit damage from injected text in log messages? (Choose two.)
o: Tell the model in its system prompt to ignore any instructions that appear inside logs
Use a larger model, which follows injected instructions less often
Filter out log messages longer than 200 characters
Require human approval before any action the model proposes is carried out
Keep the summarizer read-only, separate from any tool that changes devices
e: Prompt instructions and bigger models reduce injection but don't prevent it. Limiting the model's tools and requiring approval contain the damage whatever it decides.

p: An engineer pastes running configurations with type 7 passwords into a public AI chat to get help. Why is this a problem even though the passwords look encrypted?
o: Type 7 is reversible encoding, so the passwords are effectively in plain text
It isn't a problem, because type 7 passwords can't be reversed
Type 7 values are salted hashes that need GPU time to crack, so the risk is low but real
The AI provider can only read type 5 and type 9 secrets, not type 7
e: Type 7 is a weak, reversible encoding, and tools decode it instantly. Redact secrets of every type, plus SNMP communities and keys, before sharing configurations.

p: How should a FastMCP tool report that a requested device doesn't exist, so the model gets a clear message?
o: print("Device not found") and return an empty list
raise ToolError("Device akl-sw9 not found") from fastmcp.exceptions
return None, which the client shows as a not-found error
Call sys.exit(1), which the client reports as a failed tool
e: ToolError sends its message to the client as a tool error, even when other exception details are masked. None or an empty result looks like success, print corrupts stdio, and exiting kills the server.

p: How can a FastMCP server tell clients, in a structured way, that a tool only reads data?
o: Register it with @mcp.resource() instead, since tools always count as writes
@mcp.tool(annotations={"readOnlyHint": True})
Write "read-only" in the tool's docstring, so the model sees it
Name the tool with a get_ prefix, so clients infer that it's read-only
e: Tool annotations, such as readOnlyHint and destructiveHint, are standard MCP metadata that clients can use, for example to skip confirmation. Names and docstrings are only hints to the model.

p: Claude Desktop starts this server as a local subprocess. Which values fill blanks 1 and 2?
o: 1: tool(), 2: http
1: prompt(), 2: sse
1: tool(), 2: stdio
1: resource(), 2: stdio
e: A function the model calls with an argument is a tool. A client that launches the server as a subprocess talks to it over stdio, while http is for remote clients.
